text: Loops over candidates; shrinking the search space.

Enumeration (brute force) tries every candidate answer and keeps the ones that pass a test. It is always correct if the candidate list is complete, so the only question is: is it fast enough? Count the candidates before you code.

Three ways to make enumeration fast enough: enumerate fewer variables and compute the last one from the others; tighten the bounds of each loop; change what you enumerate (sizes instead of corners, a value instead of a position).

Enumerating two corners of every rectangle is O(n²m²). A rectangle of height h and width w fits in (n − h + 1)(m − w + 1) places, so enumerating the size is only O(nm): 25 million steps for 5000 × 5000 (P2241).
Choosing all nine digits is 9! = 362 880 arrangements. But once the first number x is known, the ratio fixes the other two, so only about 900 values of x need testing (P1618).
A bool seen[10] marking array checks "each digit once" in one pass. int nums[3] = {a, b, c}; puts the three numbers in a small array so one loop visits them all.

For A + B = C only A and B are free; C = A + B. The "+" and "=" cost 4 sticks. With at most 24 sticks, each number uses fewer than 20, which keeps every number below about 1111, so two loops of ~1100 suffice (P1149).
Get the bound from the limits, then test it: trying a bigger bound must not change any answer. Precompute sticks(x) in an array if it is called millions of times.

More loop enumerations in this list: try every pair of cut lines for a three-colour flag and count the repaints (P3392); try every start cell and direction for a run of empty squares (P3654); count stick lengths, then choose the two equal sticks and the pair that adds up to them (P3799).
Every subset by binary masks, and by choose-or-skip recursion.
mask bits (c b a) subset
A set of n items has 2n subsets. Number them 0 … 2n − 1 and read each number in binary: bit i is 1 when item i is chosen.
One loop over the numbers visits every subset exactly once.
Test bit i with mask >> i & 1 . 1 << n is 2n. n ≤ 20 gives about a million subsets; checking each in O(n) is 2 × 107 steps. mask bits (c b a) subset 7 111 {a,b,c}

PERKET (P2036) needs every non-empty subset, so the loop starts at mask 1. "Choose exactly k of n" (P1036) is the same loop keeping only masks with k bits set. Splitting jobs between two people to finish soonest (P2392) tries every subset as "person A's jobs".

title: Subsets by recursion: choose or skip

text: take a skip a

Each level decides one item: take it or skip it. Choosing only increasing numbers (choose(v + 1) ) lists every combination once, already in dictionary order (P1157). The pattern take → recurse → undo is the heart of backtracking (第14章).
Every ordering with next_permutation, and by recursion with pruning.
A permutation is an ordering of all n items; there are n! of them (10! = 3 628 800). The standard library steps from one ordering to the next in dictionary order with next_permutation .
next_permutation rearranges into the next larger ordering and returns false after the largest one. Start from the sorted order and use do … while so the first ordering is printed too (P1706).
Starting from an unsorted array skips every ordering smaller than the start. Sort first.
When orderings are used as numbers ("add m to this permutation"), stepping m times with next_permutation is the whole solution; each step is fast on average (P1088).

Fill the positions one at a time; used[v] remembers which values are taken. The recursive form lets you prune: stop a branch early when the partial ordering already breaks a rule, which next_permutation cannot do.
Ten ingredients, each 1, 2 or 3 grams, adding up to n: at most 310 = 59 049 sequences, so try them all. Ten nested loops would work; recursion over the ingredient index is shorter (P2089).
Pruning: if even all 1s left would exceed n, or all 3s left could not reach it, stop this branch. The answer is identical, and far fewer calls are made.
